title: Community Conversations: Bigfoot Ranch and Pumpkin Patch
excerpt: Bigfoot has been spotted in southwest Oklahoma, at least that’s what visitors are told when they arrive at Bigfoot Ranch and Pumpkin Patch in Apache.
content:
APACHE, Okla. (KSWO) — Bigfoot has been spotted in southwest Oklahoma, at least that’s what visitors are told when they arrive at Bigfoot Ranch and Pumpkin Patch in Apache.

The ranch offers fall hayrides, fun and festivities for kids and families. Along the way, visitors might just catch a glimpse of Bigfoot.

Jamie McDaniel said young visitors know exactly where they want to go first.

“They make a beeline. They run straight for the jump pad, but then they realize that there’s a zip line over here, and they come running,” McDaniel said. “And the mazes, I don’t know, they love everything, but they do run to the jump pad first.”

Favorite attractions put unique spin on farm fun

But the jump pad has some competition. One young visitor had a strong recommendation for the slide.

“They have to go on the slide because it’s so fun,” Lennyx said.

It isn’t just any slide. It was made from an old truck that has been part of the McDaniel family for generations.

“We grew up here. This is our whole life. Fifth generation lives on this farm now, and that truck was one that my dad had used in the wheat fields, and we used it,” Jamie McDaniel said. “So it was sitting up there in the pasture, and it was a great purpose to reuse it.”

While Larry McDaniel brings the attractions to life, he said Jamie is the one dreaming them up.

“She’s the one that comes up with the different things. She tries to be unique,” Larry McDaniel said. “I know a lot of people have the same activities, but she always tries to put a different spin on it and build, instruct me to build something differently, and it’s kind of fun with the challenge of building and kind of creating something of your own.”

Working farm creates memories

Now in its fourth year, the McDaniels said the best part is watching families make memories.

“It’s fun just being able to provide this really cool atmosphere and seeing the kids excited,” Jamie McDaniel said. “We have a lot of birthday parties here. They just love it.”

Sometimes, the simplest activities bring the biggest smiles. In the sand pit, when asked what else can be done there, one child answered: “We can make holes.”

More than playtime is offered here. The ranch is a real working farm, and Larry McDaniel said it gives kids a chance to experience something they may not see back home.

“To me, a lot of kids that live in the city don’t get to experience the true farm and see the animals, be able to feed the animals and see how they really are and how they live,” Larry McDaniel said.

For schools, the experience is a little different. The ranch closes to the public during the week so field trip groups can have the place to themselves.

“We’re completely fenced in,” Jamie McDaniel said. “You can let the kids run and they don’t have to group them up and worry about the stranger dangers or them getting away because we are all fenced in.”

Kids say it best

If you ask the kids what they think of all this fall fun, their answers are pretty simple.

When asked why others should come, one child, Briar, answered: “To play.”

Another visitor, Kenny, was asked how high he could jump.

“Up to high, 3,100,” Kenny said.

With pumpkins, zip lines, animals and plenty of room to play, there is a little something for everyone.

The ranch opens to the public Fridays from 3 to 7 p.m., and Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.
